abstract_summary: Agent memory systems must discard stored information when their history exceeds a fixed token budget. Existing budget-accuracy frontiers quantify the resulting loss in accuracy, but do not distinguish irreversible losses caused by eviction from recoverable retrieval failures. We introduce the restore counterfactual,...
citation: What Eviction Destroys: A Restore-Counterfactual Audit of Forgetting in Agent Memory. Chen Shen. 2026-09-08. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08279

The restore counterfactual characterizes oracle-answerable policy errors under a memory
budget by separating what eviction destroyed, what retrieval missed, and what the reader
failed to use. These three sources of error require different remedies. For the budgeted-
memory literature, this means that budget–accuracy frontiers are not comparable unless the
read-time retrieval regime is reported. Our contribution is an instrument for this analysis; it
does not rank policies.

The abstract and conclusion reinforce that the contribution is an instrument for analysis.

evidence.excerpt:
Interpreting the decomposition requires three assumptions. For each, we explain why it is
plausible here and how it can fail.
A1 (Oracle-answerability).We score only errors for which the reader answers correctly
under clean full-gold injection. With this restriction, a scored error is one the reader could
have answered from clean gold, so the bins reflect what the budget did to the evidence
rather than the reader's inability to answer. That interpretation can fail only if the clean-gold
context is itself unanswerable, which the filter excludes by construction. The same filter also
limits what we characterize to the answerable slice of the benchmark, excluding abstention
behavior.
A2 (Judge validity).Reader and judge are both GPT-4o-mini. To check grading stability,
we calibrated the judge on 40 questions before the main evaluation, obtaining repeat self-
consistency of 1.0 against a 
[… separate evidence block …]
threshold of ≥0.90 (App. A). This certifies grading stability
but not independence from the reader. A correlated reader–judge bias would therefore
be invisible to the cross-reader check. As a separate check of grading agreement, an
independent GPT-5.5 judge re-grading a stratified sample agrees with GPT-4o-mini at 95.7%
(Cohen's κ=0.90; App. C). Both judges are OpenAI models, so a judge from a different
provider, or human annotation, would be a stronger check.
A3 (Restore tightness).Full-gold restore is the default; it makes the irreversible share an
upper bound on destruction. Three checks quantify the slack in this upper bound over
the 2,276 irreversible cases (App. C). Restoring only the surviving gold reclassifies 0.3%.
Injecting the complete retained store (100% coverage) recovers 2%, so 98% of irreversible
cases are not latent in retained memory and are consistent with genuine 
[… separate evidence block …]
destruction rather
than a retrieval miss. Finally, an equal-length placebo (non-gold content at the gold posi-
tion) flips 8.3% against 100% for the gold restore, so the bin reflects evidence availability,
not placement (8.3% upper-bounds the combined presentation and unannotated-evidence
effect).
evidence.explanation: Section 3.3 states each assumption and explains how it can fail. A2 is checked via judge self-consistency of 1.0 on 40 calibration questions and 95.7% agreement (Cohen's kappa=0.90) with an independent GPT-5.5 judge. A3 is checked with three slack quantifications: restoring only surviving gold reclassifies 0.3%, injecting the complete retained store recovers 2%, and an equal-length placebo flips 8.3% versus 100% for gold restore.
evidence.paraphrase: The validity of the three-bin interpretation rests on three stated assumptions: oracle-answerability (A1), judge validity (A2), and restore tightness (A3), each with explicit failure modes and empirical checks.

evidence.excerpt:
The measured composition indicates which component needs improvement. Under tight
budgets, improving retention takes priority over improving retrieval (R1): a better retriever
offers little benefit until more evidence is retained. The recoverable component is nonzero
but depends on the retrieval regime (R2). Budget–accuracy frontiers are therefore not
directly comparable unless their retrieval regimes are reported. At matched accuracy, no
difference in irreversible rate is detected among the tested policy pairs at a resolution of
1.2–6 percentage points (R3). The instrument identifies the limiting component but does not
select a best policy.
Limitations.The study uses a single benchmark, two readers, and one primary judge; the
audit judge shares its provider. R1/R2 and the R3 null replicate across readers; the residual
is reader-dependent. The audit requires gold labels and an 
[… separate evidence block …]
oracle-answerable filter, which
limits its use to benchmark analysis. The eviction arms are policy classes rather than the
published systems. The null is specific to the tested policies and budgets.
Ethics.Here, "destruction" refers only to the loss of task evidence through eviction. In
deployment, forgetting may be necessary to meet privacy and data-protection requirements
concerning data minimization, storage limitation, or erasure; in such cases, retaining more
information may be undesirable or disallowed. The instrument quantifies the task cost
of a forgetting decision without prescribing whether information should be retained or
deleted; the same decomposition can audit whether a required deletion incurs recoverable
or irreversible task loss.
evidence.explanation: The Discussion section explicitly lists these limitations. The authors acknowledge that a correlated reader-judge bias would be invisible to the cross-reader check because both judges are OpenAI models, and they recommend a different-provider judge or human annotation as a stronger check. The ethics discussion clarifies that 'destruction' refers only to task-evidence loss and that the instrument can audit required deletions without prescribing retention.

positive_signals: The paper's primary contribution is a restore-counterfactual metric that classifies oracle-answerable eviction errors into recoverable, irreversible, and residual categories, plus a controlled LongMemEval-S study of four eviction policies across three budgets and two retrieval regimes.

The validity of the three-bin interpretation rests on three stated assumptions: oracle-answerability (A1), judge validity (A2), and restore tightness (A3), each with explicit failure modes and empirical checks.

The destructive control, which evicts gold at approximately 3x the baseline rate, yields a significant irreversible-rate difference in all 9 contrasts (p<0.001 under the primary reader; p<0.05 across both readers), demonstrating that the statistic registers a large destructive difference.

Under top-k retrieval at 80k tokens, the two-bin irreversible share is 0.71 (CI .61-.81) for FIFO, 0.73 for random, 0.67 for redundancy-aware, and 1.00 for the destructive control, with every lower bound exceeding 0.5, supporting the claim that destruction is the majority component.

Recoverable errors occur under top-k retrieval but are absent under forced-gold injection by construction, producing significant recoverable-share gaps at 80k for FIFO (+0.29, CI .19-.39), random (+0.27), and redundancy-aware (+0.33), all significant after Holm correction (padj=.007).

Existing budget-accuracy frontier work (DeMem, BudgetMem) quantifies accuracy loss under tighter budgets but does not characterize the composition of that loss into irreversible versus recoverable failure modes, which is the gap the restore counterfactual addresses.

The study uses a single benchmark, two readers, and one primary judge; the audit judge shares its provider with the reader, and the instrument requires gold labels and an oracle-answerable filter, limiting its use to benchmark analysis.

The evaluation code was construct-validated using a deterministic substitute for model calls and is released with per-question records, with the dataset version pinned by hash and the protocol included with the artifact.
